# From lists to structs {#sec-structs}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

When R code needs to keep several related values together, it uses a list. For example, `list(mean = 0, sd = 1)` holds the two parameters of a normal distribution under names you choose, and nothing checks that the list has those names or that they hold numbers. Rust's equivalent is the struct. A struct declares its fields and their types up front, and the compiler checks every place one is created or used. This chapter compares the two, with S4's typed slots as a halfway point, and introduces the example that runs through Part II: a normal distribution, described by its mean and standard deviation. The matching chapter of the Rust book is "Using Structs to Structure Related Data" [@rustbook, chap. 5].

## A list of named values

In R, a normal distribution's parameters fit naturally in a named list:

```{r}
#| label: r-list
dist <- list(mean = 0, sd = 1)
dist$mean
dist$sd
```

In Rust, you first define a struct, then create a value of it:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-struct
struct Normal {
    mean: f64,
    sd: f64,
}

fn main() {
    let dist = Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 1.0 };
    println!("{}", dist.mean);
    println!("{}", dist.sd);
}
```

The definition names a new type, `Normal`, with two fields that are both `f64`. Like a function, it usually goes outside `main()`, where the whole program can use it. Creating a value lists each field with its value, and `dist.mean` reads a field the way `dist$mean` does in R. By convention, type names such as `Normal` are written in CamelCase, while variables and functions use snake_case.

## Checking fields and their types

An R list accepts whatever you do with it:

```{r}
#| label: r-list-loose
dist <- list(mean = 0, sd = 1)
dist$sdev
dist$m
dist$mean <- "zero"
str(dist)
```

The misspelled `dist$sdev` returns `NULL` instead of an error. The shortened `dist$m` returns the mean, because `$` matches a name by its first letters when the match is unambiguous. And nothing stops the mean from becoming a character string. All three lines run.

In Rust, mistakes like these don't compile, and the compiler reports all of them at once. This program leaves out a field, puts text in a number field, and misspells a field name:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-struct-errors
#| error: true
struct Normal {
    mean: f64,
    sd: f64,
}

fn main() {
    let missing_sd = Normal { mean: 0.0 };
    let text_mean = Normal { mean: "zero", sd: 1.0 };
    let dist = Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 1.0 };
    println!("{}", dist.sdev);
}
```

A value must give every field, each field must have its declared type, and only declared fields can be read.

## S4's typed slots

R does have a way to declare fields and their types: an S4 class. Its fields are called slots, and `@` reads them:

```{r}
#| label: r-s4-class
setClass("Normal", slots = c(mean = "numeric", sd = "numeric"))
dist <- new("Normal", mean = 0, sd = 1)
dist@mean
```

S4 rejects the wrong type and the misspelled name:

```{r}
#| label: r-s4-errors
#| error: true
new("Normal", mean = "zero", sd = 1)
dist@sdev
```

::: {.callout-tip title="The same idea in R"}
An S4 slot declaration says what a struct field says: this field exists, and it holds this type. S4 is the closest thing R has to a struct. One difference is timing. S4 finds a mistake when the line that contains it runs, which may be deep into a long job; rustc finds it before the program runs at all.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
S4 slots are looser than struct fields in two more ways. A `numeric` slot holds a vector of any length, so a normal distribution with two means and two standard deviations is a valid object. And S4 lets you leave a slot out. This class sets no default values (`setClass()` takes them in its `prototype` argument), so S4 fills the missing slot with an empty vector of the declared type and carries on:

```{r}
#| label: r-s4-loose
two <- new("Normal", mean = c(0, 1), sd = c(1, 2))
two@sd
incomplete <- new("Normal", mean = 0)
incomplete@sd
```

A Rust `f64` field holds exactly one number, and a struct has no automatic default for a field you forgot. Every field gets a value when the struct is created, or the program doesn't compile. @sec-s4 adds S4's validity checks, which can catch both problems and many others, still at runtime.
:::

## Changing a field

R can change an element of a list, and it can add new ones:

```{r}
#| label: r-list-modify
dist <- list(mean = 0, sd = 1)
dist$sd <- 2
dist$n <- 30
names(dist)
```

In Rust, changing a field requires `mut` on the variable, which then covers every field:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-struct-modify
# struct Normal {
#     mean: f64,
#     sd: f64,
# }
let mut dist = Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 1.0 };
dist.sd = 2.0;
println!("{}", dist.sd);
```

(The struct definition is the same as before, compiled but not shown.) Adding a field, as `dist$n <- 30` does in R, isn't possible. A struct has exactly the fields its definition lists.

## Printing a struct

R prints a list without being asked how. Rust doesn't know how to print a struct you've just defined, even in the debugging form:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-debug-error
#| error: true
struct Normal {
    mean: f64,
    sd: f64,
}

fn main() {
    let dist = Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 1.0 };
    println!("{:?}", dist);
}
```

The compiler's suggestion is the usual fix. Putting `#[derive(Debug)]` above the struct asks the compiler to write the printing code for you:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-derive-debug
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Normal {
    mean: f64,
    sd: f64,
}

fn main() {
    let dist = Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 1.0 };
    println!("{:?}", dist);
}
```

The `#[...]` line is an attribute, an instruction to the compiler attached to the item below it. @sec-display covers printing in full, including how to choose your own format.

## Constructors and methods

R code that works with a list like this usually comes with a constructor function and a few helpers that take the list as an argument:

```{r}
#| label: r-constructor
normal <- function(mean = 0, sd = 1) {
  list(mean = mean, sd = sd)
}

variance <- function(dist) {
  dist$sd^2
}

dist <- normal(0, 2)
variance(dist)
```

In Rust, functions that belong to a type go in an `impl` block for that type:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-impl
struct Normal {
    mean: f64,
    sd: f64,
}

impl Normal {
    fn new(mean: f64, sd: f64) -> Normal {
        Normal { mean, sd }
    }

    fn variance(&self) -> f64 {
        self.sd * self.sd
    }
}

fn main() {
    let dist = Normal::new(0.0, 2.0);
    println!("{}", dist.variance());
}
```

There are two kinds of function in the block:

- The constructor `new()` is called on the type, as `Normal::new(0.0, 2.0)`, the same way you called `Vec::new()` in @sec-vectors and `String::from()` in @sec-strings. Calling a constructor `new` is a convention, not a keyword. Inside it, `Normal { mean, sd }` is shorthand for `Normal { mean: mean, sd: sd }`, used when a variable has the same name as the field.
- The method `variance()` is called on a value with a dot: `dist.variance()`. Its first argument, `&self`, is a reference to that value, the same kind of `&` as in front of a slice (@sec-vectors), and `self.sd` reads its field. Because the method doesn't take the struct over, `dist` is still usable after the call. A method that changes a field takes `&mut self` instead (@sec-environments).

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
R's `variance()` is an ordinary function that accepts any list with an `sd` element. A method in `impl Normal` belongs to `Normal` alone. Giving several types a method with the same name and the same meaning is what S3 generics do in R and what traits do in Rust, the subject of @sec-s3-traits.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Package developer notes: lists and structs in memory" collapse="true"}
In C, an R list is a generic vector whose elements are found by position. To find one by name, code has to search the `names` attribute; *Writing R Extensions* gives a helper that loops over the names and compares each with the one requested [@r-exts, sec. 5.9.7]. A Rust struct keeps no names at runtime. The compiler turns `dist.sd` into a fixed position in memory, so reading a field involves no search.
:::

## Summary

| R | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `list(mean = 0, sd = 1)` | `Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 1.0 }`, after a `struct` definition |
| `dist$mean` | `dist.mean` |
| A misspelled name returns `NULL`; `$` matches partial names | A misspelled field doesn't compile |
| Any element can hold any type | Each field has one declared type |
| S4 slots check names and types at runtime | Struct fields are checked at compile time |
| A `numeric` slot holds a vector of any length | An `f64` field holds one number |
| S4 fills a missing slot with a default, an empty vector unless the class sets one | Every field must be given a value |
| `dist$sd <- 2`, and `dist$n <- 30` adds an element | `dist.sd = 2.0` with `let mut`; fields are fixed |
| Lists print themselves | `#[derive(Debug)]`, then `{:?}` |
| A constructor and helper functions | An `impl` block with `new()` and methods |
